summary: This informational document defines the xml2rfc version 3 vocabulary, an XML-based language for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It is heavily derived from the version 2 vocabulary and obsoletes the v2 grammar described in RFC 7749.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7991 defines version 3 of xml2rfc, an XML vocabulary for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It gives authors elements for document structure and content, and describes how tools check and turn that XML into other formats.

subtitle: The XML vocabulary that RFC and Internet-Draft authors use to prepare documents for publication.

tldr.problem: Authors need a defined XML vocabulary for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts and for tools to process those documents.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7991 defines xml2rfc version 3: a set of elements and attributes, a RELAX NG grammar, and an expected workflow with a preparation tool and formatters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7991 obsoletes RFC 7749, is Informational, and has been updated by RFC 9920.

facts.label: File extension
facts.value: .xml, or .rfcxml when needed to distinguish the file

today: RFC 7991 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 7749 and has been updated by RFC 9920. It defines the xml2rfc v3 vocabulary and warns that later revisions may make incompatible changes.

sections.title: Purpose and Limits of Version 3
sections.content:
RFC 7991 defines version 3 (v3) of the xml2rfc vocabulary, an XML-based language for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It obsoletes the v2 grammar described in RFC 7749 and is intended for use as part of the RFC Series format described in RFC 6949.

The vocabulary includes constructs that may not appear in a final document but can still support index generation, keyword databases, or syntax checks. The RFC expects later revisions to include changes learned from implementing publication tools, and warns implementers not to assume those changes will remain backwards-compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the tags and attributes authors use to write RFCs and Internet-Drafts in XML. Some tags help tools even when they do not appear in the finished document, and later versions may change incompatibly.

sections.title: The Main Parts of an XML Document
sections.content:
The root <rfc> element contains optional <link> elements, one <front>, one <middle>, and an optional <back>, in that order. The front matter holds the title, author details, and other metadata, and may include an abstract. The middle holds the document's main sections.

The back matter can hold references and appendices. In this context, nested <section> elements in <back> represent appendices, while sections in <middle> are the main body. A <seriesInfo> element in the front matter identifies the document series and number or name.
sections.plainLanguage: An xml2rfc document has a required front part and main body, with an optional back part. The front part identifies the document and its authors; the body holds its sections, and the back can hold references and appendices.

sections.title: Elements, Attributes, and Validation
sections.content:
Section 2 describes the vocabulary's elements and attributes. An element describes a kind of document content or structure; an attribute supplies a value for an element. Attributes are optional unless the RFC marks them mandatory. Many elements can have a document-wide unique anchor, and every element can carry xml:lang, xml:base, or both.

The vocabulary is defined in prose and based on the RELAX NG schema in Appendix C, written in RELAX NG Compact Notation. The schema supports automated validity checks, but some constraints appear only in prose. Processing tools collapse horizontal whitespace and line breaks to one space, except inside <artwork> and <sourcecode>; tabs are prohibited inside those two elements.
sections.plainLanguage: Elements name the parts of a document, and attributes give those parts extra information. A RELAX NG schema can check many rules, but readers and tools must also follow rules stated in the prose.

sections.title: Text, Lists, Artwork, and Source Code
sections.content:
Version 3 separates several kinds of content. Authors can use <dl>, <ul>, and <ol> for lists, with <li> for each item. Elements such as <strong>, <em>, <tt>, <sub>, and <sup> mark character formatting.

<artwork> preserves spacing and line breaks for diagrams and other artwork, and can refer to a graphics file with src; its text can provide a fallback description. The new <sourcecode> element is for source code and formal languages. The new table elements provide table structure similar to HTML, including optional table headings and footers that are intended to repeat across page breaks.
sections.plainLanguage: Use different tags for lists, emphasis, artwork, code, and tables. Artwork keeps its spacing for diagrams, while source code has its own tag and is shown in a fixed-width font.

sections.title: Anchors and Links to Document Parts
sections.content:
An anchor gives an element a unique name that authors can target with <xref>. Processing tools also add a generated pn value to many elements; that value can identify a part that has no author-supplied anchor. In HTML output, anchors and generated values become identifiers, so their names must not overlap.

The <relref> element links to a section or anchor in a cited reference. Its target identifies the reference, and its section identifies the part of that document; a relative value can supply a relative URI. Formatters that support links use these values to create a link to the referenced location.
sections.plainLanguage: An anchor gives a document part a name that another part can point to. A relative reference links to a specific section or named part in another document.

sections.title: What Changed from Version 2
sections.content:
The design aims to make starting and editing documents easier and to support tools that convert v2 documents to v3. A v2 document is intended to be valid v3, though some v2 features are deprecated. The RFC says ease of use matters more than preserving every part of the older grammar.

Version 3 adds list elements, inline formatting, HTML-like tables, block quotations, source code, relative references, and other elements and attributes. It replaces the DTD-based grammar with a RELAX NG grammar. Deprecated elements remain supported as input to v3 tools, but the RFC says they are likely to be removed from those tools in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 3 keeps much of version 2 so older documents can still be used. It adds tags for common document features and marks some older tags for eventual removal from tools.

sections.title: Preparation and Formatting Tools
sections.content:
The expected workflow uses a prep tool to check a v3 document, add or change attribute values, and produce a prepared document that is valid v3. The RFC describes expected modes for RFC processing, Internet-Draft submission, author diagnostics, and consolidation of external resources. It points to RFC 7998 for the prep tool's description.

Formatting tools take prepared documents and produce HTML, PDF, plain text, or other representations. The RFC also expects tools to support XInclude, which lets an XML document include information from elsewhere. It says XInclude should generally be used instead of external inclusion through entities or XML processing instructions.
sections.plainLanguage: A preparation tool checks the XML and creates a prepared file for the next step. Formatting tools turn that file into output such as HTML, PDF, or plain text.

sections.title: Security Risks in Document Processing
sections.content:
Tools that process xml2rfc files must treat file names and paths from the document as untrusted. An artwork name can be used as a local file name, and an artwork src can cause a tool to read a local file. The RFC warns tools to reject dangerous paths, especially absolute paths outside the current directory.

A type value can encourage a formatter to extract artwork or source code. Extracting content may be safe, but rendering it or executing it without checking it first is unsafe. When a processor fetches content from an external URL, the RFC says it should use a sandbox so any impact stays localized; XML processing security guidance also applies.
sections.plainLanguage: Document-processing tools must check file paths and extracted content before using them. The RFC recommends a sandbox when tools fetch material from an external address.

sections.title: Unicode and Author Names
sections.content:
Because the format is based on XML, it can represent arbitrary Unicode characters in text. The RFC Series Editor may still restrict which characters are allowed in a particular RFC; the rules for those restrictions are covered in RFC 7997.

Several author and address elements have an ascii attribute for an ASCII equivalent. The <author> element has equivalent fields for a full name, initials, and surname. These fields let the primary value use a native script while processed documents can also show an ASCII equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: XML can represent text in many writing systems, though the RFC Series Editor can set character limits for a document. Authors can provide an ASCII version of names and address details alongside the main text.

sections.title: Media Type and Link Relation Registrations
sections.content:
RFC 7991 updates the registration for the application/rfc+xml media type. It has no required parameters and an optional charset parameter with the same meaning as for application/xml. The registered file extension is .xml, or .rfcxml when needed to distinguish it from other XML files.

The RFC also registers the link relation convertedFrom. It describes a link to a document that was later converted into the document containing the link, such as an Internet-Draft that became an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The document identifies xml2rfc files with a media type and file extension. It also defines a link label for pointing to an earlier document that was converted into the current one.
